title: Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive
body_html:
Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive

Theorem (competitive). Under a uniformly random arrival order, the sample-then-threshold online auction obtains expected welfare at least one quarter of the maximum valuation.

The sample-then-threshold auction

The sample-then-threshold auction is an instance of the online single-item auction (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction) with an explicit threshold rule that splits the bidders into two phases:

  • Observe phase — the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ arrivals face no acceptable price and are rejected unconditionally.
  • Acceptance phase — every later arrival faces a threshold whose price is the largest value seen in the observe phase and whose identity tag is the identity of that value's holder (breaking ties among value-equal observers by identity).

In short: watch half the bidders go by, then sell to the first later bidder who beats the best one watched (using identity to break ties at the maximum).

Statement

Fix the number of bidders $n \ge 2$, an injective identity assignment $g$ (so all bidders carry distinct identities), and nonneg valuations $v$. Assuming bidders bid truthfully (their bid equals their value),

$$ \frac14 \cdot \max_i v_i \;\le\; \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma \in \mathrm{Perm}(n)} \mathrm{welfare}\bigl(g\circ\sigma,\; v\circ\sigma\bigr), $$

where the average over permutations $\sigma$ of the bidder indices models the uniform random arrival order.
proof_html:
Let $\mathrm{MAX} = \max_i v_i$. Order the bidders by the lexicographic order on the pairs $(v_i, g_i)$: value first, identity second. Identity injectivity makes all pairs distinct, so there is a unique lex-argmax bidder $a$ and a unique lex-second bidder $c$ with $a \ne c$ and $a$ strictly above $c$ in this order. Note that $a$ attains the maximum value $\mathrm{MAX}$ — value strictly dominates the lex order, so a lex-argmax is also a value-argmax.

The proof has three pieces.

The favourable event

Call an arrival order $\sigma$ favourable when the lex-argmax $a$ lands in the second (acceptance) phase and the lex-second $c$ lands in the first (observe) phase.

Welfare equals MAX on every favourable arrival order

Suppose $\sigma$ is favourable. In the observe phase $c$ is one of the bidders seen, so the observed lex-max — and hence the threshold posted at the start of the acceptance phase — is at least the pair $(v_c, g_c)$.

Now walk through the acceptance phase one bidder at a time.

  • Every pre-$a$ acceptance-phase arrival is rejected. Any such bidder $j \ne a$ has $(v_j, g_j)$ strictly below $(v_c, g_c)$ in the lex order (since $c$ is the lex-second among all bidders), and so $(v_j, g_j)$ is also strictly below the threshold. Strict lex-below fails the acceptance test on both possibilities — strict on the price, or equal price with insufficient identity tag — so $j$ is rejected.
  • The lex-argmax $a$ is admitted. When $a$ arrives the threshold is unchanged (it can only have been refreshed by earlier acceptance-phase arrivals, all of which were rejected). The pair $(v_a, g_a)$ is lex-strictly above the threshold (which sits at most at $(v_c, g_c)$), so the acceptance test succeeds. Welfare equals $v_a = \mathrm{MAX}$.

The favourable event has probability at least 1/4

Each ordered pair of positions for $a$ and $c$ — $a$ in any of the $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ second-half slots, $c$ in any of the $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ first-half slots — extends to exactly $(n - 2)!$ favourable permutations (the remaining bidders are placed freely). So

$$ \bigl|\{\sigma : \sigma \text{ favourable}\}\bigr| \;\ge\; \lceil n/2 \rceil \cdot \lfloor n/2 \rfloor \cdot (n-2)!. $$

The elementary inequality $4\,\lceil n/2 \rceil \cdot \lfloor n/2 \rfloor \ge n(n-1)$ then gives

$$ 4\,\bigl|\{\sigma : \sigma \text{ favourable}\}\bigr| \;\ge\; n(n-1)\,(n-2)! \;=\; n!, $$

so at least one quarter of all permutations are favourable.

Assembly

Welfare is always nonneg, and equals $\mathrm{MAX}$ on every favourable permutation, so the sum over all permutations is at least $\frac{1}{4} n! \cdot \mathrm{MAX}$. Dividing by $n!$ gives the bound.

Remarks

Why identity injectivity, not value injectivity

The hypothesis is that identities are distinct, not that values are. This is the natural assumption: each bidder is a distinct entity, but multiple bidders may share a value. The identity tag of the threshold (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction) is what makes this hypothesis enough. Two consequences:

  • The lex-argmax and lex-second of the pairs $(v_i, g_i)$ are unique even when values collide.
  • The "every pre-$a$ acceptance-phase arrival is rejected" step uses lex-strict comparison, which only needs identities to be distinct at value ties, not values to be globally distinct.

Without the identity tag the theorem would need the mathematically unnatural global hypothesis that all bidders have distinct values; see the definition node for the full design rationale (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction).

Why it matters

Together with the deterministic impossibility (No Deterministic Constant Competitive Ratio), this closes the picture for the online single-item auction: worst-case arrival order admits no constant competitive ratio, yet random arrival order restores a constant one. It is the single-item, prophet-free instance of the classical secretary phenomenon — observe a constant fraction of the input, then take the first item that beats it.

Lean formalization

In EconCSLib, the auction is auction, defined as a SingleItemAuction B F whose threshold rule reads:

threshold h := if h.length < n/2 then ⊤ else ↑(toLex (maxPairFold h))

where maxPairFold folds the rejection history to find the lexicographic maximum of the seen (value, identity) pairs, starting from $(0, \bot)$ (this requires [OrderBot B]).

The favourable event is captured by the structure Favorable, which records the index of the lex-argmax in $\sigma$, the index of the lex-second, the maximality witnesses (v_is_max, g_is_max_among_ties, lex_is_second, lex_second_lt_max), and the position constraints (max_in_second_half, second_in_first_half). The lemma welfare_eq_max_of_favorable packages the inductive walk through the acceptance phase via the helper welfareAux_favorable, which threads the rejection history through welfareAux. The lemma favorableSet_card_ge counts favourable permutations using Finset.exists_max_image to extract the lex-argmax and lex-second under the Prod.Lex order, the bijection $\sigma \mapsto \sigma^{-1}$ to reduce to a position-pair count, and the combinatorial lemma count_Q for the slot-placement multiplicity. The top-level theorem competitive assembles welfare_nonneg, welfare_eq_max_of_favorable, and favorableSet_card_ge into the 1/4 bound.

References

  • [Roughgarden 2016, Lecture 2, Problem 2.1(c)] Tim Roughgarden, Twenty Lectures on Algorithmic Game Theory, Cambridge University Press. Random-order (secretary-style) analysis of the online auction.
